item.title: Vitamin C can’t cure colds – how a Nobel Prize winner’s claims were disproved
item.description: Multiple studies conducted since Linus Pauling’s analysis showed that vitamin C has a minimal effect on colds.
item.content:encoded:
From the first hint of cold winter mornings, supermarkets and pharmacies begin heavy marketing to coax us to stock up on vitamin C to get through the cold and flu season.

But where did that idea come from?

As we’ll see, it’s a story including a Nobel Prize winner, a book and some claims that don’t quite stack up.

Nobel Prize winner writes a book

Linus Pauling was a chemist from the United States who won two Nobel Prizes. One was in 1954 for chemistry, for his research into chemical bonds. The other was in 1962 for peace, for his activism against nuclear weapons testing.

He was not a dietitian or an infectious disease physician. But that didn’t stop him publishing a book on vitamin C and colds in 1970. This book is widely credited with the skyrocketing sales of vitamin C at the time, a trend that continues today.

In this book, Pauling said we should consume high doses of vitamin C, around 1,000-2,000 milligrams a day for good health, and even more to prevent a cold.

His recommendations were said to be initially from one placebo-controlled trial in children on a ski camp in the Swiss Alps. He then analysed a further four studies conducted after his claims.

item.title: ‘Chakmak’: A poetry collection about tribal life is essential for the re-education of the urban mind
item.description: Poet Ramesh Karthik Nayak was awarded the 2024 Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar for these poems.
item.content:encoded:
Some time ago, I spent a week staying among and interacting with the staff and the students at three remote tribal schools of Dahanu Taluka in Maharashtra’s Palghar District. I stayed long enough to catch bursts of ebullience on the school playground day after day. That ebullience is the very force of nature running through their veins – the nature that they don’t see themselves as being distinct from.

Ramesh Karthik Nayak’s poetry collection Chakmak is replete with bursts of the very same ebullience throughout this book. It is best manifested in the way Nayak constructs his imagery. The abstract nouns or the qualitative adjectives that account for the lock, stock, and barrel of much of the imagery in mainstream poetry are not his weapons. Instead, it is the action verbs that convey the images in his poems. Consider the way Nayak captures nightlife in a forest:

Bats and owls
ransack the night.

He strips the image to the bare minimum and then lets the verb carry it. All the vividity and the vivacity of that image come from that one word: ransack. Even when an image is loaded with sensory words, it is his verbs that carry the image:

The ambience
of pollen dust-stained fireflies
churn darkness.

item.title: ‘Blue Flag’ tag push for India’s beaches is violating coastal rules, evicting local communities
item.description: Development projects to meet the certification requirements are disrupting the dynamic ecosystem of beaches.
item.content:encoded:
On the evening of February 19, 58-year-old Anbukarasi sat alone in the usually bustling marketplace at the coconut grove in Puducherry’s Eden beach. Until a couple of days earlier, local residents were running temporary stalls selling fried fish, boiled corn, cucumbers, mangoes, toys and hats to tourists visiting the beach.

But on Sunday, February 15, the commissioner of the Ariyankuppam Commune Panchayat issued an eviction notice demanding that the stall owners vacate the area by Monday. On Tuesday, the police came and started pulling the tarpaulins off the 50-odd stalls. “They took about a hundred of us to the police station at Ariyankuppam,” said Anbukarasi, “We asked them to not remove the shops and that this is our only livelihood and we need our beach.”

After some negotiation and the involvement of a local legislator, the stall owners were given an extension till the 19th. While most stall owners left by then, Anbukarasi stayed put, urging every visitor to buy the cucumbers and boiled corn that she was selling. “I’m making the most of the three days that I am allowed to run my shop,” she said. “This is my only source of income other than the Rs 2,500 [a month] I get from the government...

A total of 5,211 drivers were tested during a statewide inspection campaign that began on August 20, including 3,942 in Mumbai. On the third day of the campaign, drivers found to lack functional knowledge of Marathi were served notices and given one month to learn the language.

The inspection campaign began after the August 15 deadline for taxi and auto-rickshaw drivers to acquire functional knowledge of Marathi had expired.

item.title: ‘London Falling’: A captivating investigation into a 19-year-old’s double life and death in London
item.description: Ostensibly about the death of a teenager, Zac Brettler, the book is a matryoshka doll of stories with charming rogues, liars, criminals and the nefarious types.
item.content:encoded:
In September, 2015, Patrick Radden Keefe wrote about Ken Dornstein, whose older brother David had perished in Pan Am Flight 103 which had exploded mid-air, six miles above the earth. The debris fell over Lockerbie, Scotland. Over many decades, Ken kept trying to solve the murder mystery of his brother’s death. Who was responsible?

If a writer’s career is a sum of its parts, then all of Patrick Radden Keefe’s career has led to London Falling, his most recent non-fiction book. Ostensibly about the death of a teenager, Zac Brettler, in 2019, the book is a matryoshka doll of stories with charming rogues, liars, criminals and various nefarious types. At the heart of the tale, the centre of it is the grief and bewilderment of Zac Brettler’s parents, both children of Holocaust survivors, thoroughly decent folks who realise that their teenage son, while alive, was a fabulist of the highest order. Zac went around lying to everyone about his family and wealth. Using the name Zac Ismailov, he claimed to have been the son of a Russian oligarch.

item.title: After Maharashtra, Karnataka bans analogue paneer for one year
item.description: The order also applies to food business operators that use the non-dairy paneer as an ingredient.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration department has banned the manufacture and sale of analogue or non-dairy paneer marketed as paneer in the state for one year, the Hindustan Times reported.

Analogue paneer is a non-dairy or partially synthetic substitute for paneer. It replaces milk fat and milk solids with cheaper vegetable oils, making the dairy products cheaper.

A notification issued on August 17 prohibits the processing, packaging, storage, transportation, distribution and wholesale or retail sale of analogue paneer in the interest of public health.

The ban also applies to food business operators that use analogue paneer as an ingredient. Restaurants, food manufacturers, caterers and other food establishments have been prohibited from using, storing, supplying or selling such products in food preparation.

However, the notification does not cover standardised food products for which the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has prescribed separate quality standards. Products such as frozen desserts, processed cheese and mixed-fat spreads, which have their own recognised standards, are excluded from the ban.

The Food Safety Division said enforcement measures would be carried out across Karnataka to ensure compliance with the order.

On July 30, Maharashtra banned the production and sale of analogue paneer for one year, citing public health concerns.

item.title: Sunday book pick: The specific curse of dating men in ‘Nearly All the Men in Lagos Are Mad’
item.description: Published in 2021, this is Nigerian writer Damilare Kuku’s debut book.
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria’s biggest city, Lagos, resembles a proper madhouse in Damilare Kuku’s 2021 debut book, the short story collection Nearly All the Men in Lagos Are Mad. It is hot and populous, and everyone’s hustling for more money or better sex. The men take shortcuts for both and women trip over themselves trying to make sense of this collective madness. Time and again they realise there is no substitute for extreme caution.

A heady romancescape

The 12 stories in the collection describe the experiences of cisgender women in various stages of heterosexual relationships. Women of all age groups and socio-economic classes suffer the madness of their men – but few take it lying down, finding ways to make the most out of their compromised circumstances. The title is catchy and relatable, and women in every city in the world will nod in approval. The men are a diverse set too, from cheating pastors to mama’s boys, from gay men to “alpha” Whites, men who endlessly pursue and those who are emotionally unavailable. Lagos’s heady romancescape often sweeps up unsuspecting women in its unique madness.

item.title: The 19th-century Indians who nurtured a self-reliant scientific culture in colonial India
item.description: The story of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science that helped an Indian win the Nobel Prize in Physics is a snapshot of these untiring efforts.
item.content:encoded:
One afternoon in 1907, a young accountant named Chandrasekhar Venkata Raman walked into the laboratory of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science at 210 Bowbazar Street in Calcutta.

Though he had a passion for the sciences, colonial India offered no stable careers in the field, so Raman had joined the Indian Finance Service.

But after work, Raman started a series of pathbreaking experiments – first in sound, then in optics – at the laboratory of the IACS, an institution that had been established just over three decades earlier specifically to popularise science and encourage Indians to conduct research at a time when such opportunities were scarce.

Soon, Raman (who would go on to become the secretary of the IACS) along with his associate KS Krishnan started experiments related to light. The phenomenon he recorded, where light changes its wavelength when scattered by molecules of a liquid, is called Raman Effect.

In 1930, this work earned Raman the Nobel Prize in Science, making him the first person from Asia to win this award.

item.title: 8.7 crore young Indians are ‘NEET’ – not in education, employment or training, says NITI Aayog
item.description: They need affordable or subsidised training and financial support, said the think tank in a report.
item.content:encoded:
An estimated 8.7 crore Indians aged 15 to 29 are not studying, working or undergoing training, said a report by the NITI Aayog, the main public policy think tank of the Union government.

The report, titled Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047, is based on data from the 78th round of the National Sample Survey conducted in 2021. It classifies India’s workforce and learners into five categories: those attending school, going for tertiary education, involved in formal and informal work, women and those not in education, employment and training, or the NEET youth.

“NEET youth are constrained by the absence of income and the sunk cost of prior education,” said the report. “Students often cannot layer paid skilling onto existing financial commitments.”

This group, along with women, needs affordable or subsidised training and financial support, underlined the NITI Aayog. It also said that skilling programmes should be linked to the demand of emerging sectors and self-employment opportunities.

“Across segments, the ability to combine learning with earning remains a central requirement,” it said.

The report further pointed out that only 8.25% of persons who have graduated from college are employed in roles aligned with their qualifications.

“Limited exposure to practical learning and industry-aligned training continues to constrain employability, even among formally educated youth,” it said.

item.description: As a government that prided itself on setting the narrative struggles to stay on top of it, ministers have been asked to step up their social media presence.

At a Cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Union ministers were handed report cards. They were not being assessed for their performance as ministers but on how active and effective they have been on social media.

Each minister was ranked based on an evaluation of their social media presence between May 1 and August 15, a period that includes the nationwide youth protests over the alleged irregularities in competitive exams.

Each minister was compared not just with their Cabinet colleagues, but also against leaders of other political parties on platforms such as Instagram, X and Facebook, according to reports.

The parameters included average number of posts per day, engagement per post, the number of likes, number of followers their accounts have and the overall level of public interactions.

The ministers were told to step up their activities on social media and focus more on expanding their presence online.

item.title: ‘Writing to dazzle can be a fatal mistake of the preoccupation with writerly craft’: Saikat Majumdar
item.description: An interview with the author of ‘Open Intelligence: Education Between Art and Artificial’.
item.content:encoded:
Having read several of Saikat Majumdar’s novels and a couple of his non-fiction books, I consider him one of those rare contemporary writers who move seamlessly across fiction, nonfiction, and academia – embodying the spirit of a true literary polymath. What I find particularly compelling about his writing is the way it inhabits both intimacy and ideas with equal ease. His novels delve into love, desire, friendship, memory, cities, and the shifting textures of modern life with emotional acuity, while his nonfiction carries the same depth through sharp insight and elegant prose. Across genres, his writing has consistently challenged and moved me, often leaving me with unexpected reflections long after I’ve finished reading.

In a conversation with Scroll, Majumdar talked about his latest book Open Intelligence: Education Between Art and Artificial, the value of narrative intelligence, why we urgently need to re-evaluate our intellect, and more. Excerpts from the interview:

item.title: ‘India’s Forests, Real and Imagined’: Forests as literary-political figures across three millennia
item.description: Alan Johnson’s book complements environmental histories and anthropological studies with a literary-critical focus.
item.content:encoded:
India’s Forests, Real and Imagined: Writing the Modern Nation by Alan Johnson is an ambitious work of literary ecocriticism that attempts to trace the figure of the forest across approximately three millennia of Indian literary history. It looks at the ancient Sanskrit epics and Tamil Sangam poetry, proceeds to colonial-era nationalism and progressive realism, and then to contemporary postcolonial fiction and Indigenous writing.

Ecological realities and fictitious constructs

The book has been published by Bloomsbury Academic as part of a series in environmental humanities and literary studies and is the result of years of research supported by a Fulbright-Nehru award alongside extensive institutional backing from Idaho State University. It is undeniable that the book has had an incredible journey fuelled by evident passion and considerable scholarly range, but there are tensions in a humongous project that aims to accomplish so much within a relatively compact frame.

The introduction of the book invites its readers on an aerial survey of the Indian subcontinent as it might have looked, around 3000 years ago. Johnson moves south from Himalayan Oak Valleys to the forests bearing sal, sandalwood, teak, and neem. item.title: Ramachandra Guha: Historian Sumit Sarkar took his scholarship beyond the confines of the academy
item.description: He was was one of several prabasi Bengali intellectuals who helped make Delhi University the foremost academic institution in all of South Asia.
item.content:encoded:
In a late essay reflecting on his intellectual journey over the decades, Sumit Sarkar remarked: “So far, we Indian historians have written the histories that we wanted to write, following no agenda but our own. That seems to be a fast-vanishing luxury.”

In a long and very productive life, Sarkar – who was born in Calcutta in 1939 and died in Delhi earlier this month – had to confront three historical agendas imposed by others. The first was a dogmatic Marxism which viewed the past through a narrow economistic lens, and was very influential in Sarkar’s hometown (his father, also a historian, was a member of the Communist Party of India).

The second was the interlinked trend of post-modernism and post-colonialism which viewed history as fragmented and culturally relative, and focused on texts and discourses rather than the lived experiences of people in the past.

The third was the religious majoritarianism of the sangh parivar, which glorified Hindus and demonised Muslims, and despite – or perhaps because of – its Manichaeism gained ideological and political ascendancy in the 1990s and beyond.

item.title: 1 in 3 US workers have ‘disposable’ jobs: An economist outlines the public costs
item.description: Their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the costs otherwise associated with lay-offs and fair treatment at work.
item.content:encoded:
When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.

When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.

These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 US workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.

I am a labour economist. In my new book, Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment, I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.

item.title: Can intense interiority in a book leave the reader thoroughly alienated from the narrator’s life?
item.description: ‘I could step into their world for a bit, but I could never really immerse myself.’
item.content:encoded:
This summer I picked up my friend’s half-read copy of Eula Biss’ Having and Being Had and read a hundred pages curled up on his sofa. I did not particularly find it relatable – she is an essayist and educator living in a palatial house in Chicago, and the book is mostly about her own complicated relationship with owning a house and the material reality that emerges from it. But I was hooked.

After that I read Rachel Cusk’s Outline and Annie Ernaux’s Exteriors in quick succession. The books don’t have much in common; they are not all memoirs, and some resemble the literary style of a confessional. But they all wanted me to see the author as someone with a voice, an opinion, a style, a vision. The structural nature of these books reminded me of a conversation with an acquaintance – I could step into their world for a bit, but I could never really immerse myself. Ultimately it was the inevitable solipsism of their world, where there was no respite from their mind – everything existed in the world that solely belonged to them. item.title: Thinking is a sport, not a chore: Why children’s literature creators will win the war against AI
item.description: A children’s author makes a case for rejecting AI.
item.content:encoded:
Disclaimer: The following text is entirely human-authored. No “outside” help was sought to outline the piece. Editing was not outsourced to a “foreign hand”. Research was strictly restricted to gossip, Google and good ol’ social media skulking. Synonyms were deployed the old-fashioned way (many thanks, Roget’s International Thesaurus). Sentences were completed unassisted. Deadline was missed by a mile. Slap on that “100% unaided by AI” sticker already.


With that out of the way, let’s get started on the much-dreaded, oft-debated, forever-relevant subject of AI.

My first brush with it? Many, many decades ago. In the presence of a responsible adult. For a short story.

“AIEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE!!!!!” went a particularly excitable character from the aforementioned work of fiction.

I fondly remember my English teacher’s remarks lovingly scribbled in the margins: “Way too many exclamation marks”, “Couldn’t figure out the rest. Would’ve been easier to read hieroglyphics”, and “Save doodles for art class”. Moral of the story? Using AI in creative writing does not lead to gold star glory.

Cut to the present.

Poet, essayist, fiction writer, translator, editor – Udayan Vajpeyi occupies a singular place in contemporary Indian literary life. Widely regarded as one of the most original voices in Hindi, his writing has consistently expanded the language’s imaginative and intellectual horizons.

Some of Vajpeyi’s best-known works are Kuchh Vakya, Pagal Ganitagya Ki Kavitayen, Sudeshna, Door Desh Ki Gandh, Saatavan Button, Charkhe Par Barhat, and Patjhar Ke Paon Ki Mehndi, among others. His novel Qayas, recently translated by Poonam Saxena into English as Love Is Participation in Eternity, has introduced him to a wider readership. As a translator, he has brought writers such as Borges, Chekhov, Octavio Paz and Shuntaro Tanikawa into Hindi, opening new aesthetic and philosophical pathways for readers.

Alongside his literary work, Vajpeyi spent more than four decades teaching Physiology at Gandhi Medical College, Bhopal. The coexistence of medicine and literature, science and imagination, appears to have shaped a distinctive sensibility in his writing, one deeply attentive to memory, grief, the human body and the unseen dimensions of experience.

item.title: How English artists depicted India as exotic land ripe for colonial rule

In 1825, English artist George Chinnery left Calcutta for Macau, chased away by his disgruntled wife Marianne and his creditors. He’d been based in India for the past 23 years, having previously lived in Hyderabad and Dacca.

Besides running a debt of around Rs 30,000 (£232 today), Chinnery was, according to one Dictionary of National Biography, a “penniless fornicator” and “begetter of an uncertain number of illegitimate Chinnerys white, brown and yellow”.

While he became famous as a portraitist, Indian landscapes also take pride of place in Chinnery’s legacy. His vision of an early morning in the Bengal countryside projects an image of peace and harmony far removed from the realities of colonial India under the British Empire.

My own interest was in the energetics of marine fisheries: the input-output balance of energy in that world. Ethanol was one of the clearest examples Alier used of that balance being falsified elsewhere.

Energetics involved converting everything – a litre of diesel, an hour of a fisherman’s labour, a kilogramme of fish – into the same currency: the calories, or kilocalories, of energy each one represents.

Simple bookkeeping can then be done: for every calorie that goes into fishing, how many calories of food come back out? When the return is high, the fishery is productive. When it costs more energy to catch the fish than what the fish give back as food, there is a deficit – even if the market still calls the catch a success.

item.title: Cats were domesticated thousands of years ago. Are they finally getting tamer?

Around 15 years ago, I created a Facebook page for my cat, Sandi. Friends thought it was weird. Today, social media accounts for cats attract millions of followers, cats travel in backpacks and prams, and surveys consistently show that the overwhelming majority of owners regard their pets as family.

I’ve previously written about how cats became domesticated. But domestication isn’t necessarily a process with an endpoint. Could it still be continuing today?

Examples from wildlife suggest that adaptation to living alongside people can continue long after animals first encounter humans.

Research led by biologist Kevin Parsons at the University of Glasgow provides one of the clearest examples of this process. In 2020, Parsons and his team compared the skulls of urban and rural red foxes from London and the surrounding countryside, and found consistent differences between the two populations.

Urban foxes had shorter, broader snouts and smaller braincases – the rounded part of the skull that encloses the brain. These are changes that often accompany domestication. The researchers suggest that city life may favour foxes that are less fearful of people and better at exploiting food and shelter provided by humans.

item.title: Lucknow’s gleaming Gomti riverfront symbolises urban progress, but what about ecological resilience?
item.description: The project offers critical lessons for the future of urban water management.
item.content:encoded:
At first glance, the Gomti Riverfront appears to be a triumph of urban transformation. Gleaming promenades, landscaped gardens, cycling tracks, and illuminated riverbanks have recast the Gomti as a symbol of a moderniding Lucknow. Yet beneath this carefully curated landscape lies a more unsettling question: when cities attempt to beautify rivers, what exactly are they restoring and what are they erasing?

The Gomti Riverfront is not merely a story of infrastructure; it is a story of competing visions of development. While the project has delivered public spaces, enhanced real estate values, and a renewed civic relationship with the river, it has also narrowed floodplains, simplified habitats, and failed to address the persistent pollution flowing through the river itself.

As climate uncertainty intensifies and Indian cities increasingly turn to riverfront development as a model of urban renewal, the Gomti offers a crucial lesson. The challenge is not whether rivers should be integrated into city life, but whether they can be revived without sacrificing the ecological processes that keep them alive.

Within the larger category of Dalit writing, where can we situate Dalit women’s writing?
Dalit girls, tribal girls, and girls from the minority sections of society are educationally and economically far behind compared to girls from other sections of society. There are a lot of obstacles in the way of Dalit literature, where the authors, publishers and sellers are all Dalit writers themselves. It is very difficult for a Dalit woman writer to transcend that barrier. item.title: Singapore is culling ‘pest’ birds but their population keeps growing
item.description: Rapid urbanisation creates favorable conditions for birds like crows and pigeons to thrive as forests are lost to high-rise buildings, say experts.

On a Friday afternoon in July, a pest control officer patrols the grounds of Sungei Tengah Lodge, Singapore’s largest dormitory for migrant construction workers, picking up birds in various stages of distress. Some are twitching, others are wobbling, as if drunk.

The officer tosses the birds, which he had poisoned with baited scraps a few hours earlier, into a garbage bag. Most of them are still alive. The bagged birds will later be gassed using carbon dioxide, a culling method for “pest” birds the authorities say is “humane” – a claim contested by animal welfare groups.

Though culling may immediately trim the local population, ecologists question the long-term effectiveness of efforts to reduce urban birds, arguing that Singapore’s rapid urbanisation creates favorable conditions for them to thrive, as forests are lost to high-rise buildings.

Birds considered pests in the tropical metropolis are the common pigeon (Columba livia), Javan myna (Acridotheres javanicus) and house crows (Corvus splendens), which are not protected under the Wildlife Act and routinely culled in response to complaints from the public.

Known as “nuisance” birds, they’re framed as invasive species that are noisy and a threat to public health and local biodiversity by competing with and, in the case of crows, preying on native birds.

item.title: What the panic over Gen Z’s reading habits gets wrong
item.description: Identifying as a reader used to mean sitting alone with a book and Gen Zers are more likely to experience reading as a social activity.
item.content:encoded:
A trove of recent articles bemoan the collapse in recreational reading among younger Americans, with Covid-related reading declines, artificial intelligence and social media often described as causes.

But as the authors of “How Gen Z Discover and Consume Books,” we think many claims about Gen Z’s reading behaviours miss the mark.

Some long-standing, influential studies aren’t designed to capture how Gen Z often reads: multimodally – bouncing between print, e-book and audiobook for the same book – and on web platforms such as Wattpad, Webtoon, Kindle Unlimited, DC Universe Infinite and Marvel Comics online.

In fact, according to our 2025 data, a growing proportion of Gen Z – 66% – is identifying as readers, up 14 percentage points from 2022. In the previous 12 months, 65% of Gen Z read at least one print book, up from 59% in 2022. These findings roughly correspond with those of the Pew Research Center for the general population across all ages.

In other words, Gen Z shows us that reading isn’t dying. It’s changing.

A postdigital generation of readers

Gen Z is the first generation to grow up with internet access from an early age. In Arunachal Pradesh, conversations in mithun-rearing communities often find their way to the animal. For outsiders, one question almost inevitably follows: “How many mithuns do you own?”

When John Pei Cander was asked the same question, the enthusiasm with which he had been talking moments earlier suddenly faded. He paused before replying quietly, almost apologetically. “Now, I have just four,” he said. “During my father’s time, our family had around 30.”

John runs a successful business, owns agricultural land, and has built a concrete two-storied house, drives an SUV. His children are studying in private schools. Yet it was not these achievements that defined his pride. It was the shrinking number of mithuns his family owned. He is not alone.

Many with government jobs, thriving farms or successful businesses hesitate before revealing a single-digit number when asked about their mithuns. Their responses carried a sense of shame. Owning fewer mithuns, several people suggested, is not merely an economic reality; it was a loss of status and inheritance.

For generations, the mithun (Bos frontalis) has occupied a unique place amongst many Indigenous societies of northeast India. item.title: ‘With grace, we go to paradise’: Five poems that span the trauma and fractures of life in India
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Moplah Speaks of the River’, by Umar Nizarudeen.
item.content:encoded:
DNA

They came from the Papal State
and hadn’t been to a kindergarten
and exclaimed,
“Little men! We should be in Gulliver’s land.”
The “men” suddenly grew up
as if by mutation
and took the fathers
down the ages.

Till,
a sense of still being there
gripped them, and they hastened up
only to be frozen
in test tubes.


Truth

The blood mixed in the soil
is not lost—
God’s will reigns over planes.
The devil pollutes the day with tentacles,
the sea roars truth forever,
the son bears the father’s burden,
and love pampers rocks.
The lost wealth shall return.
In markets, fruits abound.
The bee sucks honey there.
With grace, we go to paradise.


Aura Aura Aura

Bengal!
Land of effulgence and horripilation…
Dominatrices,
flagellating momma…
Smouldering alphabets, and tear-stained cacti;
I do not know what!
Gilt-edged speech and soaring IQs,
Naxalbari and Nischindipur,
thorny-fish and mishti-doi,
swamps and stigmata!
I am your son from the desert,
Give me only…
Taka! Taka! Taka!

But what I remember most is
the day she called me
and showed me her breasts
with scales setting in
circular pyramids of
translucent flakes.
With the labyrinths exposed
inside out
like a sea anemone.

I am an albino, colourless
but all her other kids are green.

of claymore mines

I could never understand
this artistic obsession with pain.
Its sunflower blooms solar
till a woman on the internet
showed its priority
when she passed a DC current
into someone, strung up
just to take it,
writhing up and squirming

The Son Koli, a fishing community, are original inhabitants of Greater Mumbai, Navi Mumbai and Thane, in western Maharashtra. They witnessed the rise and fall of great empires, invasions, imperialism and colonialism, fight for freedom, the birth of a republic, and the hurtling of the region into hyper-urbanisation. Over centuries, the Koli fished and mended their nets in quiet fishing villages that dot the coast but in the last few decades the world around them irrevocably changed. The number of Koliwada (a traditional fishing village) are rapidly shrinking, now down to just over 275 neighbourhoods in the Mumbai megalopolis. Several Koliwadas are surrounded by high-rises and modern infrastructure, but the fisherfolk community is struggling, much like the ocean they depend on. Abujhmad, a captivating expanse of hills, woods and streams, holds a special place in the contemporary history of Bastar. One of the first journalist–researchers to explore this region was Ramesh Chandra Roy, joint editor of the Ranchi-based anthropology journal Man in India. item.title: Friendship paradox: Why young people feel ‘too connected to connect’
item.description: Many report struggling to build friendships that provide a genuine sense of closeness, belonging and support.
item.content:encoded:
You know what’s happening in the lives of dozens of people. A friend from school has just had a baby. Someone you follow online recently got engaged. A colleague has returned from a holiday. Messages and updates arrive constantly. Yet when you’re having a difficult week, deciding who to call feels surprisingly hard. You’re connected – but you don’t feel it.

This paradox is increasingly familiar to many young adults. Despite being more connected than any previous generation, many report struggling to build friendships that provide a genuine sense of closeness, belonging and support. Young people have been described as “too connected to connect”.

You might feel you have more connections than ever before, but those connections can feel shallow, rushed and carefully staged. Relationships abound, but authenticity – the ability to be yourself – feels scarce.

In my own work, I’ve seen this in children who contort themselves into particular roles or identities to preserve family connection. Or in spouses and partners who hide parts of themselves to maintain a facade or status quo in a marriage or romantic relationship.

In essence, it is a form of conditional love: the idea that we are only lovable if we present particular sides of ourselves, while keeping others carefully edited or hidden away....

item.description: Trump has also, according to the book and exhaustive reporting by journalists, abused his power to enrich himself and his family.
item.content:encoded:
Not long after the Second World War, the Jewish, German-born political philosopher Leo Strauss coined the term reductio ad Hitlerum. It suggests that simply comparing something to Adolf Hitler does not inevitably taint it with the Nazi dictator’s terrible crimes. Hitler was a vegetarian, but that doesn’t make all vegetarians bad people.

When the internet arrived several decades later, attorney Mike Godwin updated Strauss. “As an online discussion grows longer,” he said, “the probability of a comparison involving Nazis or Hitler” increases.

item.title: Bangladesh to Nepal, revolutions toppled regimes but lasting change is elusive
item.description: Gen Z movements are swift and successful but struggle to do the slow work of institutional transformation.
item.content:encoded:
Two years after Bangladesh’s July uprising, the country’s greatest political lesson is no longer about how an authoritarian government fell.

It is about why replacing a government proved far easier than rebuilding a state. This is not simply Bangladesh’s story. It is becoming the defining political paradox of Generation Z across the world.

From Dhaka to Kathmandu, from Tunis to Colombo, young people have demonstrated an extraordinary ability to mobilise millions, but a much more limited ability to translate revolutionary momentum into durable institutional change.

The question is no longer whether young people can bring down governments. They clearly can. The real question is whether they can redesign the machinery of the state after the celebration ends.

The July uprising will remain one of the most remarkable moments in Bangladesh’s democratic history. Millions of citizens, led largely by students and young activists, united behind a simple objective.

The movement gathered enormous public sympathy after the killing of Abu Sayeed, whose death became a powerful symbol of state violence. Within weeks, a government that had ruled for fifteen years collapsed under unprecedented public pressure.

item.content:encoded:
India is now Asia’s least-preferred stock market, replacing Indonesia, Bloomberg quoted a Bank of America survey of fund managers as having shown on Wednesday.

The Indian stock market has been one of the world’s worst performers this year.

The survey found that 32% of fund managers were allocating a smaller share of their portfolios to Indian stocks. The biggest concern among investors was that there are not enough listed Indian companies with a strong presence in the artificial intelligence sector, Bloomberg quoted the survey findings as saying.

Weak economic growth was the second-biggest concern. The lack of policy reforms to improve the business environment in the country and high valuations of the stocks have also contributed to the cautious view of Indian equities, the findings said.

The survey conducted between August 7 and August 13 received responses from 98 panellists managing $272 billion in assets.

Indian stocks have declined in the past two weeks despite an improving earnings forecast of companies, Bloomberg reported.

India was last ranked as the least-preferred market in Bank of America’s survey in May. At the time, rising energy costs had put pressure on the country’s growth outlook following the United States-Iran war, which spiked global crude oil prices.

When I talk about Henry Lawrence and Jeremiah Brasyer, the first thought that comes to most people’s minds is, “Those firangis, how can you have anything good to say about them, especially now when we’ve finally thrown them out?” But listen to the story and then decide for yourself what you think of these two British men.

It was July 2, 1857, two months into the Bengal Army uprising, two months of upended lives in a sweltering colony where natives and colonisers alike found their certainties crumbling. For the first time in over one hundred years, the British officers and civil servants who had assumed colonial rule to be their right and duty were afraid of what was going to happen to them.

They were ridiculously outnumbered as civilians, of course, but the Bengal Army was also over seventy per cent non-European. The most critical resource that we have is time. We all have limited time on this planet. How we make use of it determines the legacy that we create. Many of us know what truly matters to us, and yet we invest time in inconsequential activities. The distraction caused by our devices and social media is a significant cause that interferes with our desire to realise our full potential.

For example, we know that we need to put in a lot of time and effort to learn an important new skill, and yet we do not find the time to do so. Instead of taking responsibility for this, we keep blaming external factors for our failures. Many of us also suffer from procrastination. We keep putting off important work and fill our day with various distractions, which will not help us move towards our goals. Excessive Internet surfing, engaging in pointless debates, gossip and politicking are examples of time wasters.
